what_its_for: Amantadine is used to treat Parkinson's disease and movement problems (like uncontrolled movements) caused by certain medicines. It was also once used to prevent and treat influenza A (flu), but it is no longer recommended for the flu because most flu viruses are now resistant to it.
how_to_take: Take amantadine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. If you take the extended-release (long-acting) capsules or tablets, swallow them whole — do not crush, chew, or split them. Take your doses at the same time each day to keep a steady amount of medicine in your body. Do not suddenly stop taking amantadine without talking to your doctor first, as this could make your condition worse.
dosing: Your dose will depend on your condition and how your kidneys are working. For Parkinson's disease, adults usually start at 100 mg once or twice daily, and the dose may be adjusted by your doctor. Extended-release forms are often taken once daily at bedtime. Your doctor will find the right dose for you — never take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store amantadine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about medicine take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking amantadine, as it can increase dizziness and other side effects. Be careful driving, operating machinery, or doing anything that requires alertness until you know how this medicine affects you — it can cause dizziness, confusion, or blurred vision. Avoid getting up too quickly from sitting or lying down, as this medicine can cause a drop in blood pressure and make you feel lightheaded. Avoid going out in very hot weather or doing things that cause heavy sweating, as amantadine can affect your body's ability to handle heat.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you notice: hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), confusion, agitation, or unusual behavior; thoughts of suicide or self-harm; severe dizziness or fainting; swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles; a purplish or bluish skin discoloration (mottled skin); sudden urge to gamble, eat, shop, or have sex more than usual (unusual impulse-control problems); signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face or throat; or if you stop urinating or notice a major change in urination.
when_it_works: Some people notice improvements in their Parkinson's symptoms within a few days, but it may take up to 2 weeks to feel the full benefit. Talk to your doctor if you do not notice any improvement after 2 weeks. Keep taking the medicine even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects like confusion, hallucinations, and dizziness. Lower doses are often used and monitored carefully. Kidney problems: If your kidneys do not work well, your body may not clear this medicine properly, and you may need a lower dose. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on your kidney function. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Amantadine may harm an unborn baby, so the risks and benefits should be discussed with your doctor. Breastfeeding: Amantadine passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medicine. Children: Safety and dosing in children depends on the condition being treated. Follow your doctor's specific instructions.
